unit.title: Develop and apply conversational skills in a foreign language

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain why staff in a salon or hotel spa that serves visitors should learn some Spanish, and how it helps the client's safety as well as the service.
essays.modelAnswer: Many visitors to Jamaica, and many guests at the big resorts, come from Spain, Mexico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and other Spanish-speaking countries. A few words of Spanish, such as "Buenos días, bienvenida al salón", make the client feel welcome and respected, and she is more likely to relax, enjoy the service, buy aftercare products and come back. It also helps safety. Before a colour, wax, facial or massage the stylist or therapist must ask about allergies, skin problems, medicines and pregnancy. If the client understands the questions, such as "¿Tiene alguna alergia?", she can answer truthfully and the worker can avoid a reaction or burn. During the service the worker can check "¿Le duele?" or "¿Está bien el agua?". Good communication also means fewer mistakes with the style or length the client wants, and fewer complaints for the business.
markingPoints: Many guests and visitors to Jamaica speak Spanish
Makes the client feel welcome and respected, so she returns and buys more
Consultation questions (allergies, health, skin) are understood and answered truthfully
Comfort and safety checks during the service (pain, heat) are understood
Fewer mistakes and complaints about the result

essays.stem: A Spanish-speaking client arrives at the salon desk. Explain, with the Spanish you would say and its meaning, how you would welcome her, find her booking and show her where to wait.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stand, smile and greet her with the right greeting for the time of day, for example "Buenos días, señora" (Good morning, madam) or "Buenas tardes" in the afternoon. I would say "Bienvenida al salón" (Welcome to the salon). Then I would ask "¿Tiene cita?" (Do you have an appointment?) and "¿Cómo se llama?" or "¿Su nombre, por favor?" (Your name, please?). I would find her booking and confirm the service and time, for example "Una manicura a las once" (A manicure at eleven). If she must wait I would say "Siéntese, por favor" (Please sit down) and "Espere unos minutos" (Wait a few minutes), and offer water. When the stylist is ready I would say "Pase, por favor" (Come in, please) and show her the way. I would use "usted" all the way through, speak slowly and smile.
markingPoints: Stands, smiles and uses a greeting that fits the time of day
Welcomes the client and asks if she has an appointment
Asks for and checks her name and the booked service and time
Asks her to sit or wait politely, then invites her in
Gives correct meanings and uses the polite form throughout

essays.stem: Describe the consultation questions you would ask in Spanish before a hair colour or a waxing treatment, and explain why each one matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would ask "¿Tiene alguna alergia?" (Do you have any allergies?), because colour, wax and some products can cause a reaction. Before a permanent colour I would ask "¿Se hizo la prueba de alergia?" (Have you had the skin test?), because the maker's instructions often ask for a skin test about 48 hours before; without it I must not colour. I would ask "¿Toma algún medicamento?" (Do you take any medicine?), because some medicines and skin creams make the skin thin or sensitive, which matters for waxing. I would ask "¿Tiene la piel sensible?" (Is your skin sensitive?) and look for cuts, sunburn or rashes on the area. For waxing I would ask "¿Está embarazada?" (Are you pregnant?) only in a private, polite way, because it changes how the skin reacts. I would write the answers on her record card and ask her to sign it.
markingPoints: Asks about allergies, with the correct Spanish
Asks about the skin (patch) test before colour, as the maker requires
Asks about medicines or skin conditions, and checks the area for cuts, sunburn or rashes
Explains why each question matters for safety
Records the answers on the client's card and has it signed

essays.stem: A Spanish-speaking client's answers about her health are not clear before a chemical service. Explain what you would do and why.
essays.modelAnswer: I would not go ahead until I was sure I understood her. A chemical service such as a relaxer, colour or chemical peel can burn or cause an allergic reaction if the client has a cut scalp, an allergy or a skin problem. First I would slow down, speak clearly and use simple questions with "sí" or "no" answers, such as "¿Alergia, sí o no?". I would show her the consultation form, point to each question and use pictures or a phrase card. I could use a translation app, checking the meaning with her and keeping her details private. If it is still not clear I would ask a colleague or supervisor who speaks Spanish, or ask her companion to help translate. If we still cannot be sure, I would explain politely that we cannot do the chemical service today and offer a safe service instead, then record what happened.
markingPoints: Does not start the chemical service while the answers are unclear
Explains the risk (burns, allergic reaction, contraindications)
Uses simple yes/no questions, the form, pictures or a translation app
Gets help from a Spanish-speaking colleague, supervisor or companion
If still unsure, politely offers another service and records it

essays.stem: Describe the instructions you would give in Spanish during a shampoo at the basin or a facial, and say what each one means.
essays.modelAnswer: At the basin I would say "Siéntese aquí, por favor" (Sit here, please) and then "Incline la cabeza hacia atrás" (Tilt your head back). I would check the water with "¿Está bien el agua?" (Is the water all right?) and ask "¿Más fría o más caliente?" (Colder or hotter?). At the end I would say "Levántese despacio" (Get up slowly). For a facial I would say "Acuéstese boca arriba, por favor" (Lie face up, please) and "Cierre los ojos" (Close your eyes) before I cleanse or steam. If I needed her to keep still I would say "No se mueva, por favor" (Please keep still). I would finish with "Ya terminamos" (We have finished). I would always speak slowly, use "por favor", and show with my hands what I mean.
markingPoints: Gives a correct instruction to sit or lie in the right position
Gives a correct instruction to tilt the head or close the eyes
Checks the water temperature or comfort in Spanish
Gives the meaning of each phrase correctly
Speaks politely and slowly, with gestures to help

essays.stem: Explain how you would check a client's comfort in Spanish during a service, and what you would do if she says something is too hot or that it hurts.
essays.modelAnswer: During the service I would check often by asking short questions: "¿Está cómoda?" (Are you comfortable?), "¿Le duele?" (Does it hurt?) and "¿Está bien la presión?" (Is the pressure all right?) during a massage. Before wax touches her I test it on my own inner wrist, and I would ask "¿Está bien la temperatura?". If she says "¡Está muy caliente!" (It is very hot!) or "Me duele" (It hurts), I would stop at once. I would remove the heat or the product, look at the skin and cool the area with cool running water if it is red or burnt. I would apologise with "Lo siento" and tell my supervisor. I would not carry on until the cause was fixed and she agreed. Any reaction or burn goes in the accident record.
markingPoints: Asks comfort questions often, in correct Spanish
Tests wax or heat on own inner wrist before it touches the client
Stops at once if the client says it is hot or hurts
Checks the skin and gives correct first aid (cool running water)
Apologises, reports to the supervisor and records it

essays.stem: Describe how you would take a telephone booking in Spanish, including the service, the day, the time and the client's name.
essays.modelAnswer: I would answer with the salon's name and "Buenos días, ¿en qué le puedo servir?" (Good morning, how can I serve you?). When the caller says "Quisiera una cita" (I would like an appointment), I would ask "¿Para qué servicio?" (For which service?), for example "un corte", "una pedicura" or "un masaje". Then I ask "¿Qué día?" (Which day?) and "¿A qué hora?" (At what time?), check the book and offer a time, for example "El jueves a las dos" (Thursday at two). I would ask "¿Su nombre, por favor?" and a phone number, and ask her to spell her name if needed. I would write it all on the booking sheet, then repeat it back slowly to check it: day, time, service and name. I would end with "Gracias, hasta el jueves" (Thank you, see you Thursday).
markingPoints: Answers politely with a greeting and the salon's name
Asks which service, in Spanish
Asks and agrees the day and the time, with correct Spanish
Takes the name and phone number and writes them on the booking sheet
Repeats the details back to confirm, then closes politely

essays.stem: Describe how you would finish a service in Spanish: showing the result, giving aftercare advice, taking payment and saying goodbye.
essays.modelAnswer: I would show the client the finished work in the mirror, including the back with a hand mirror, and ask "¿Le gusta?" (Do you like it?). If she wants a change I would fix it. Then I would give simple aftercare, for example after a facial "Use protector solar" (Use sunscreen), or after a pedicure "Cuidado, el esmalte está fresco" (Careful, the polish is wet). I would take her to the desk and say the price clearly, writing the number down too, and ask "¿Paga en efectivo o con tarjeta?" (Cash or card?). I would give her the receipt and change and offer to book the next visit: "¿Quiere otra cita?". Finally I would say "Gracias por su visita" (Thank you for your visit) and "Hasta la próxima" (Until next time), with a smile.
markingPoints: Shows the result in the mirror and asks if she likes it
Gives simple aftercare advice in Spanish
States the price clearly (written down too) and asks how she will pay
Offers to book the next appointment
Thanks her and says goodbye politely

essays.stem: Explain how pictures, colour charts, written numbers and gestures can help a stylist or therapist who knows only a little Spanish, and give an example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: When I know only a few words, other ways of showing help us both understand. Pictures of hairstyles, nail designs or brow shapes let the client point to what she wants, so I do not guess the length or shape. A colour chart for hair colour or nail polish lets her choose the exact shade, and I can say the colour word, such as "rojo" or "rubio", to check. Writing numbers down, such as the price J$4,500 or the time 3:30, stops mistakes with numbers I might say wrongly. Gestures help too: I can show with my fingers how much hair to cut, or point to the basin and say "Aquí, por favor". I should always check back by asking "¿Así?" (Like this?) before I start, and stay patient and polite.
markingPoints: Pictures or a style book: client points to what she wants
Colour chart: client chooses the exact shade
Writing numbers (price, time) avoids number mistakes
Gestures and pointing, used politely
Checks back with the client before starting

essays.stem: Explain the main points of good manners and culture to remember when serving Spanish-speaking clients, including how to address them.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use the polite form "usted" and titles such as "señora", "señor" or "señorita" with the surname, not the first name, until the client asks me to use her first name. Many Spanish speakers have two surnames, such as López García; the first one is normally used with the title, so I would say "Señora López". Some guests greet with a handshake or a light kiss on the cheek; I respond warmly but stay professional and do not start it myself. I would ask before I touch, for example before a massage or when I move the client's head, and keep her covered and private. Clients come from many countries, so words can differ; I would not laugh at an accent or a different word. I would be patient, smile and speak slowly and clearly.
markingPoints: Uses usted and titles with the surname
Knows that two surnames are common and the first is used with the title
Responds to greetings warmly but professionally
Asks before touching and respects privacy
Respects different countries, words and accents; stays patient

practical1.title: Spanish consultation card and salon or spa service role play
practical1.brief: Your group will make a Spanish–English consultation card (on card, a poster, or a phone or computer screen) for a salon or spa. It must show at least 20 phrases, with the Spanish spelt correctly (accents, ñ, ¿ and ¡) and the English beside each, grouped as: welcome and booking; consultation questions (allergies, skin test, medicines, skin or scalp problems); instructions during the service; comfort checks; and aftercare, payment and goodbye. Then act out a visit by a Spanish-speaking client for one service the group chooses: a shampoo and blow-dry, a manicure, a facial or a hand and arm massage. Act it in four stages: welcome at the desk; consultation; the service with instructions and comfort checks; and aftercare, payment and goodbye. Every member plays the stylist or therapist in at least one stage and speaks Spanish in it; the others play the client or take notes. The assessor may play the client and give one answer that needs a follow-up question. Only practise the hands-on part with a partner who agrees, using plain products. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the notes to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Card or poster paper and markers, or a phone or computer
A Spanish–English dictionary or phrase book
The salon's consultation form (English) to copy questions from
Reception desk, booking sheet and a pen
Salon chair, basin or treatment couch, towels and plain products for the chosen service
A hand mirror and a price list
photos: The finished consultation card, close enough to read
Stage 2: the consultation, with the form
Stage 3: the service, hands and work area only
Stage 4: aftercare advice, payment and goodbye
The group's notes on who played each part
checklist: Helped make the card: phrases correct, with accents and meanings
Greeted the client with the right greeting for the time of day and used usted
Asked at least two consultation questions in correct Spanish and understood the answers
Gave at least one clear instruction and one comfort check in Spanish
Gave aftercare advice or took payment and said goodbye in Spanish
Spoke slowly and clearly, and checked the client understood
Worked hygienically and treated the partner with respect
safety: Only use plain products (no chemical services) in the role play
Clean and disinfect tools and use fresh towels for each partner
Ask before you touch, and stop if the partner is uncomfortable
Photos show only hands and the work area, unless the person agrees and the Centre allows it

practical2.title: Spanish service menu and telephone bookings
practical2.brief: Your group will make a service menu in Spanish and English for a hotel salon or spa (on a poster, a printed sheet or a screen). It must list at least eight services, such as a haircut, a wash and blow-dry, braids, a manicure, a pedicure, a facial, waxing and a massage, each with the Spanish name, the English name, the time it takes and a price in J$ (the assessor gives the prices, or the group uses the Centre's price list). Add opening days and hours in Spanish. Then act out telephone bookings. Each member takes at least one call in Spanish from a caller (another member or the assessor): greet, find out the service, agree the day and time, take and spell the name and a phone number, write it on the booking sheet, repeat the details back and say goodbye. One call must be a change of booking to another day. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the booking sheet and the menu to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Poster paper and markers, or a computer or phone
A Spanish–English dictionary or phrase book
The Centre's price list, or prices from the assessor
A booking sheet or appointment book, one per member
Two phones (or toy phones) for the role play
photos: The finished service menu, close enough to read
Each member taking a booking call
The changed booking, crossed out and rewritten neatly
The group checking each booking against the menu
checklist: Helped make the menu: Spanish service names, days and hours spelt correctly
Answered the call politely in Spanish with the salon's name
Asked for the service, day and time in correct Spanish
Took the name (spelt) and phone number and wrote them clearly
Repeated the details back to confirm them
Handled the change of booking correctly
safety: Use made-up names and numbers, not real clients' details
Keep booking sheets private: do not leave them where others can read them
Sit comfortably and take short breaks from the screen
Treat every caller and team member with respect
